screens.title: Caching blockchain data
screens.narratorSegment: Caching means keeping a local copy of frequently used data so your app can serve it quickly without asking the chain each time. In dApps this often includes immutable values such as token names, tokenURI strings, or historical metadata. A cache can live in localStorage for long-lived, cross-session values, in IndexedDB for larger or structured data, or in an in-memory store like a global state (Redux, Zustand) for fast session-only reads. A practical rule is to tie cache freshness to a block number or timestamp. For example, if a tokenURI is immutable, you can cache it indefinitely; if a token balance changes often, use a short TTL such as a few seconds and combine the cache with an event subscription for updates. A common misconception is that caching always increases complexity; in reality, targeted caching reduces network load and often simplifies UI state by avoiding repeated pending states. Implementation examples include checking cache first, validating TTL, and falling back to an RPC call if missing or stale. When you design cache invalidation, prefer explicit updates on relevant events rather than blind expiry for critical user balances. How might your app decide which values are safe to cache?

keyIdea.text: Cache immutable or slowly changing data locally; use short TTLs and event-based invalidation for frequently changing values.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Caching blockchain data
What caching is and why it helps
Caching stores a copy of data locally to avoid repeated RPC requests. It reduces latency and network cost when data is stable or semi-static.
Cache locations: localStorage, IndexedDB, in-memory stores like Redux/Zustand.
Freshness: tag cached items with timestamps or block numbers to decide validity.
Invalidation: prefer event-driven updates where possible instead of blind expiries.
Key Takeaway

Cache the stable values and keep short-lived caches for volatile data, combining with event subscriptions when available.

Example: tokenURI caching
When rendering an NFT list, fetch tokenURI once per token, store it in IndexedDB or a global in-memory cache, and reuse it across renders and sessions for immutable metadata.
Common mistake
Caching dynamic data like balances without TTL or event updates can display stale values and confuse users.
Check your understanding
Is token metadata immutable in your app? If yes, prefer long-lived caches; if no, prefer short TTLs and subscriptions.

screens.title: Reduce redundant blockchain calls
screens.narratorSegment: Redundant calls happen when the same data is fetched repeatedly across renders or components. A simple three-step flow prevents waste: first, check your component state or global store for the needed data; second, check a cache layer like localStorage or an in-memory cache with a freshness check; third, if still missing or stale, issue an RPC call. Another effective strategy is to batch independent view calls into one request using a Multicall contract. Batching drastically reduces the number of round trips to a node and reduces total latency. For example, fetching balances for five ERC-20 tokens for a single account can either make five separate RPC calls or a single Multicall aggregate call with five inputs. The misconception here is that fewer calls always mean stale data; instead, combine batching with a short cache TTL and event subscriptions to remain fresh. When designing your flow, measure both the number of network requests and the end-to-end time to first meaningful paint, so you balance freshness with responsiveness. Reduce redundant blockchain calls means always prefer local state and cache checks before issuing rpc calls, and batch independent reads using multicall where possible.. In practical terms, check local state first, batch requests, then call rpc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Three-step fetch flow
Apply a predictable order: component state → cache with TTL → RPC call or Multicall aggregate.
1
Check local state
If data is already in your component or global store, reuse it to avoid network calls.
2
Check cache with freshness
Validate timestamp or block number before trusting cached results.

Call RPC or Multicall
Use Multicall to batch many view calls into one request when appropriate.
Example scenario
A wallet UI needs five token balances. Instead of five separate balanceOf calls every render, check state, consult a short cache, or issue one Multicall aggregate to retrieve all five balances at once.
Why this improves UX
Batching and caching reduce perceived load time, avoid UI flicker, and reduce the chance of rate limiting from node providers.
Misconception
Batching does not remove the need for freshness checks. Combine with TTLs and subscriptions for best results.

screens.title: Implementing Multicall
screens.narratorSegment: A Multicall contract lets you bundle many read-only calls into a single RPC request. This is especially useful when you need many balanceOf or tokenURI calls at once. The common pattern builds an array of call objects with a target address and encoded call data, then sends them to the Multicall aggregate function and decodes the returned bytes. The key advantage is fewer network round trips and lower aggregated latency. A practical gotcha is decoding the returned bytes correctly and handling failed calls gracefully — Multicall3 returns success flags per call, so check them. Here is a short code walkthrough that shows creating callData using your web3 instance, calling multicallContract. methods. aggregate(calls). call(), and decoding returnData. Compare the timings between many individual promises and one Multicall call; you will typically see a single aggregated response complete much faster than multiple sequential RPCs. Remember to adjust for token decimals when converting raw uint256 balances into human-friendly values. Implementing Multicall means use multicall to reduce rpc round trips; handle per-call success/failure and decode return bytes carefully.. In practical terms, refactor multiple view calls into a single multicall aggregate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Implementing Multicall
Code pattern
Create call objects, call aggregate, decode results, and map to tokens.
// Build calls
const calls = TOKEN_CONFIG.map(token => ({
  target: token.address,
  callData: web3.eth.abi.encodeFunctionCall(ERC20_ABI.find(m => m.name === 'balanceOf'), [account])
}));

// Single aggregate RPC
const { returnData } = await multicallContract.methods.aggregate(calls).call();

// Decode results
returnData.forEach((result, i) => {
  if (result.success) {
    const decoded = web3.eth.abi.decodeParameters(['uint256'], result.returnData);
    balances[TOKEN_CONFIG[i].name] = web3.utils.fromWei(decoded[0], 'ether');
  } else {
    balances[TOKEN_CONFIG[i].name] = 'Error';
  }
});
Example result
When fetching five balances, the Multicall approach yields one network request and a single latency bound, often faster than parallel or sequential individual RPCs.
Pro tip
When tokens have different decimals, decode raw numbers first then apply token-specific decimals before formatting for display.
Edge case
If a Multicall returns empty bytes or fails, handle it gracefully by showing an error state for that token rather than breaking the entire UI.

screens.title: Node providers: Infura & Alchemy vs self-hosted
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a node provider affects performance and reliability for your dApp. Running your own full node gives maximal decentralization and control but is resource-intensive and can be slower for many clients unless you invest in scaling and caching. Managed providers such as Infura and Alchemy offer load balancing, caching layers, stable WebSocket endpoints, and developer dashboards that make large-scale reads more reliable. They often cache common RPC requests, lowering latency for repeated queries. A misconception is that managed providers are only useful for production; during development they also save time by providing stable endpoints and faster event subscriptions. When deciding, weigh the need for self-sovereignty against the operational cost. If your dApp serves many users and requires archival data or stable WebSockets for real-time updates, a managed provider often delivers better UX with less operational overhead. Always plan for rate limits, and implement local caching and Multicall to reduce the number of requests you make to these providers. screens.title: Real-time updates: WebSockets vs polling
screens.narratorSegment: Polling is a simple way to check for new data, but it is often inefficient and increases load both on the client and the node. A better approach for real-time feeds is to use WebSocket subscriptions such as web3. eth. subscribe('logs') for events like Transfer. Subscriptions maintain a persistent connection and push events as they arrive, eliminating repeated getPastEvents polling and reducing latency. In practice, use polling only when WebSocket support is unavailable or as a fallback. Also combine subscriptions with a short cache to limit UI churn: when an event arrives, update the cache and affected components rather than re-fetching entire data sets. A common pitfall is not handling reconnects or missed events; implement logic to re-sync a small historical window on reconnect. For example, if your feed missed a few blocks while offline, fetch events from the last confirmed block number to the current block to reconcile state. This hybrid approach keeps data fresh without overwhelming the network. Real-time updates: WebSockets vs polling means prefer websocket subscriptions for real-time feeds and use short re-sync windows on reconnect to avoid missed events.. In practical terms, use subscriptions for live data and avoid inefficient polling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Why subscriptions win
Subscriptions push events as they occur, reducing redundant requests and improving real-time responsiveness.
Use web3.eth.subscribe('logs') for Transfer events and similar logs.
On reconnect, fetch a short window of past events to reconcile missed messages.
Fallback to HTTP polling only when WebSockets are unavailable, and choose a longer interval to limit load.
Example
A transfer feed should subscribe to Transfer logs. When a log arrives, update the cache for only the affected accounts rather than reloading the entire transfer history.
Check your understanding
How would you reconcile missed events after a temporary network drop? Answer: re-sync a short historic range and apply updates incrementally.

screens.title: React performance: state management and memoization
screens.narratorSegment: React performance in a dApp focuses on keeping renders minimal and predictable. Use global state for shared blockchain data and avoid passing large objects down many props. Tools like React. memo help prevent child components from re-rendering when their inputs haven't changed. useCallback stabilizes function references passed to children, and useMemo caches computed values such as filtered lists of tokens. A common mistake is prematurely optimizing and wrapping everything in memo — instead, profile and apply memoization where re-renders occur frequently or lists are long. Also avoid storing transient UI state in global stores when local component state would be sufficient. For long lists, combine memoization with virtualization to render only visible items. When a blockchain update arrives, update the minimal slice of state required; this reduces the number of affected components and keeps the UI snappy. A representative pattern is storing token balances in a keyed object and updating only the affected key when a new balance arrives. In practical terms, avoid unnecessary re-renders with selective updates and memo hooks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Virtualization and lazy loading
screens.narratorSegment: When displaying long lists of blockchain data, rendering every item at once can cause slow initial load and janky scrolling. Virtualization libraries like react-window or react-virtualized render only the items visible in the viewport, keeping DOM size small and interaction smooth. Lazy loading defers non-essential components or routes until they are needed, reducing initial bundle size and speeding up the first meaningful paint. For example, an NFT gallery might initially render a small visible page and progressively fetch and render more items as the user scrolls. Pair virtualization with batching of metadata requests using Multicall to avoid making dozens of independent network calls as new items appear. A common pitfall is virtualizing a list without limiting network calls per scroll event; debounce network requests so scrolling doesn't trigger excessive RPC traffic. Together, virtualization and lazy loading dramatically improve perceived performance for large datasets. Virtualization and lazy loading means only render visible items and defer heavy route or component loads; debounce network activity triggered by scrolling.. In practical terms, render only what the user sees and defer heavy components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Debouncing, throttling, and optimistic UI
screens.narratorSegment: User inputs that trigger blockchain requests can create many unnecessary RPC calls. Debouncing delays a function until the user stops typing for a short period, while throttling limits how often a function runs over time. Use these patterns on search fields, address lookups, and filtering controls that would otherwise call view functions rapidly. For transactions where immediate confirmation is not required, optimistic UI updates can provide instant feedback by updating client state before the transaction is mined. Implement optimistic updates carefully: present a pending state, and write rollback logic to revert changes if the transaction fails. A common misconception is that optimistic updates hide failures; instead, they should surface pending status and gracefully handle rollback. Combine debouncing with a cached search index or partial client-side filtering to make address and token searches feel instantaneous without flooding the node provider with requests. Debouncing, throttling, and optimistic UI means use debouncing and throttling to limit rpc frequency, and use optimistic ui with clear pending and rollback paths.. In practical terms, reduce unnecessary rpc triggers and give fast feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Efficient data retrieval and state management
screens.narratorSegment: Efficient retrieval in a dApp combines a one-time initial fetch with ongoing event-driven updates. A recommended pattern: 1) fetch initial data with getPastEvents or a set of view calls and cache the results; 2) subscribe to relevant events via WebSocket for real-time changes; 3) when events arrive, update the local cache and only re-render affected components. This flow avoids repeating full fetches and keeps the UI synchronized with the chain. A concrete example: display a token transfer list by fetching recent Transfer events for the first load, caching them, and subscribing to incoming Transfer logs to append new items. If a reconnect happens, re-sync using a small block range to catch missed events. A misconception is to fully rely on subscriptions without a safe initial snapshot; always seed your app state with a recent historical fetch so you have a known starting point and can apply events incrementally from there. Efficient data retrieval and state management means seed state with an initial fetch, then keep it updated via subscriptions and minimal cache updates on each event.. In practical terms, combine initial fetch, event subscriptions, and cache updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Performance in a dApp is the sum of many decisions: how often you call the chain, which node you use, and how your frontend renders results. In this lesson you will learn practical ways to reduce perceived latency by caching stable blockchain data, batching view calls with a Multicall contract, choosing a reliable node provider, and applying React optimizations like memoization and virtualization. We will also cover event-based updates via WebSockets, so you can avoid expensive polling. For example, instead of fetching the same token metadata every time a list renders, you will learn to store immutable tokenURIs locally and fetch them once. You will also see how Multicall can combine many balance queries into a single RPC request and why that matters for user experience. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to identify bottlenecks, implement a simple in-memory cache, integrate Multicall for bulk reads, and apply a set of React performance techniques. As you move through the screens, ask yourself which data in your app changes frequently and which can be safely cached.

These learning objectives describe concrete skills you will practice. First, you will learn to identify common performance bottlenecks in dApps, such as repeated RPC calls, inefficient rendering, and polling when event subscriptions would be better. Second, you will implement caching strategies for blockchain data, deciding when to store immutable metadata locally and when to use short-lived caches for rapidly changing values. Third, you will understand how node providers like Infura and Alchemy improve reliability through load balancing, caching, and WebSocket support, and when to prefer them over a self-hosted node. Finally, you will apply frontend optimization techniques specific to React dApps — using memoization, lazy loading, virtualization, debouncing, and optimistic UI updates. Each objective pairs a clear ability with why it matters and a small mnemonic to help you remember the pattern. Practicing these skills will let you trade off freshness and speed deliberately, so users experience responsive apps even when block confirmations take time.

Beyond concept knowledge, you'll practice strategies that directly change user experience. You will implement caching policies and decide cache lifetimes based on data volatility. You will measure the effect of individual vs. batched RPC calls and compare response times. You will configure event subscriptions to replace polling and maintain up-to-date state with minimal network load. The chapter culminates in a hands-on activity: refactor a TokenBalances component to first demonstrate the naive per-token calls, then refactor to use Multicall, and finally add a short-lived in-memory cache. This progression shows the real impact in measured time and network requests. Throughout, you will learn common mistakes to avoid, for instance caching data that changes frequently or relying on HTTP polling for real-time feeds. These practice objectives prepare you to instrument real dApps for speed, reliability, and a smoother user experience.

Caching means keeping a local copy of frequently used data so your app can serve it quickly without asking the chain each time. In dApps this often includes immutable values such as token names, tokenURI strings, or historical metadata. A cache can live in localStorage for long-lived, cross-session values, in IndexedDB for larger or structured data, or in an in-memory store like a global state (Redux, Zustand) for fast session-only reads. A practical rule is to tie cache freshness to a block number or timestamp. For example, if a tokenURI is immutable, you can cache it indefinitely; if a token balance changes often, use a short TTL such as a few seconds and combine the cache with an event subscription for updates. A common misconception is that caching always increases complexity; in reality, targeted caching reduces network load and often simplifies UI state by avoiding repeated pending states. Implementation examples include checking cache first, validating TTL, and falling back to an RPC call if missing or stale. When you design cache invalidation, prefer explicit updates on relevant events rather than blind expiry for critical user balances. How might your app decide which values are safe to cache?

Redundant calls happen when the same data is fetched repeatedly across renders or components. A simple three-step flow prevents waste: first, check your component state or global store for the needed data; second, check a cache layer like localStorage or an in-memory cache with a freshness check; third, if still missing or stale, issue an RPC call. Another effective strategy is to batch independent view calls into one request using a Multicall contract. Batching drastically reduces the number of round trips to a node and reduces total latency. For example, fetching balances for five ERC-20 tokens for a single account can either make five separate RPC calls or a single Multicall aggregate call with five inputs. The misconception here is that fewer calls always mean stale data; instead, combine batching with a short cache TTL and event subscriptions to remain fresh. When designing your flow, measure both the number of network requests and the end-to-end time to first meaningful paint, so you balance freshness with responsiveness. Reduce redundant blockchain calls means always prefer local state and cache checks before issuing rpc calls, and batch independent reads using multicall where possible.. In practical terms, check local state first, batch requests, then call rpc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Multicall contract lets you bundle many read-only calls into a single RPC request. This is especially useful when you need many balanceOf or tokenURI calls at once. The common pattern builds an array of call objects with a target address and encoded call data, then sends them to the Multicall aggregate function and decodes the returned bytes. The key advantage is fewer network round trips and lower aggregated latency. A practical gotcha is decoding the returned bytes correctly and handling failed calls gracefully — Multicall3 returns success flags per call, so check them. Here is a short code walkthrough that shows creating callData using your web3 instance, calling multicallContract. methods. aggregate(calls). call(), and decoding returnData. Compare the timings between many individual promises and one Multicall call; you will typically see a single aggregated response complete much faster than multiple sequential RPCs. Remember to adjust for token decimals when converting raw uint256 balances into human-friendly values. Implementing Multicall means use multicall to reduce rpc round trips; handle per-call success/failure and decode return bytes carefully.. In practical terms, refactor multiple view calls into a single multicall aggregate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing a node provider affects performance and reliability for your dApp. Running your own full node gives maximal decentralization and control but is resource-intensive and can be slower for many clients unless you invest in scaling and caching. Managed providers such as Infura and Alchemy offer load balancing, caching layers, stable WebSocket endpoints, and developer dashboards that make large-scale reads more reliable. They often cache common RPC requests, lowering latency for repeated queries. A misconception is that managed providers are only useful for production; during development they also save time by providing stable endpoints and faster event subscriptions. When deciding, weigh the need for self-sovereignty against the operational cost. If your dApp serves many users and requires archival data or stable WebSockets for real-time updates, a managed provider often delivers better UX with less operational overhead. Always plan for rate limits, and implement local caching and Multicall to reduce the number of requests you make to these providers. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Polling is a simple way to check for new data, but it is often inefficient and increases load both on the client and the node. A better approach for real-time feeds is to use WebSocket subscriptions such as web3. eth. subscribe('logs') for events like Transfer. Subscriptions maintain a persistent connection and push events as they arrive, eliminating repeated getPastEvents polling and reducing latency. In practice, use polling only when WebSocket support is unavailable or as a fallback. Also combine subscriptions with a short cache to limit UI churn: when an event arrives, update the cache and affected components rather than re-fetching entire data sets. A common pitfall is not handling reconnects or missed events; implement logic to re-sync a small historical window on reconnect. For example, if your feed missed a few blocks while offline, fetch events from the last confirmed block number to the current block to reconcile state. This hybrid approach keeps data fresh without overwhelming the network.
